originalTitle: National Park Service supports Trump’s arch even though it would have ‘adverse effects’ on other DC monuments, report says – as it happened
summary: This live blog is now closed.
content: This concludes another week in the life of the second Trump administration. Here are the latest developments: Donald Trump claimed that Venezuela’s president, Delcy Rodríguez, agreed to put more than 65bn barrels of the nation’s oil reserves under “majority US control”. ICE arrested far-right activist Milo Yiannopoulos, a British-born provocateur who wrote for Steve Bannon’s Breitbart before serving as an intern for Marjorie Taylor Greene and arranging for the white supremacist Nick Fuentes to dine with Donald Trump and Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, at Mar-Lago in 2022. A new National Park Service report on Trump’s vast monumental arch acknowledges but downplays the importance of the fact that the 250ft-high structure will have adverse effects on a series of existing monuments, including views of the Washington Monument and the Lincoln and Jefferson memorials. Activists for Turning Point USA, the rightwing youth group founded by the late Charlie Kirk, were asked to stop creating viral videos of themselves heckling Democratic candidates at the Iowa state fair, in line with the fair’s regulations, according to the Iowa political reporter Laura Belin. In a fundraising email this week, the Republican candidate for the open Senate seat in Michigan, former congressman Mike Rogers, appeared to mislead supporters about his past by suggesting that he had played an active role in the killing of Osama bin Laden. US Southern Command announced on Friday that it had raided and destroyed what it called “a vessel operating as a floating refueling station in support of illicit at-sea drug trafficking operations in international waters of the Eastern Pacific”. US marines and sailors, the military’s statement said, “interdicted, boarded, searched, and cleared the vessel without incident. Individuals removed from the vessel were safely escorted to Ecuador.” US forces then sank the vessel. According to the statement, the operation was carried out “in coordination and collaboration with the Government of Ecuador”. “Intelligence confirmed the vessel, previously identified and targeted under Department of the Treasury sanctions, was operating in support of the Los Choneros violent narco-terrorist organization,” the statement added. Hours earlier, Donald Trump had boasted, in a phone call with the crew of the International Space Station, that US military operations to attack and kill “the drug people coming in by boat” was made possible by “all that information from space”. In a fundraising email this week, the Republican candidate for the open Senate seat in Michigan, former congressman Mike Rogers, appeared to mislead supporters about his past by suggesting that he had played an active role in the killing of Osama bin Laden, the leader of al-Qaida who was shot and killed in a US military raid on his compound in Pakistan in 2011. “When I served as a U.S. Army officer and an FBI Special Agent, I swore a sacred oath to defend the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic,” Rogers wrote, according to a screenshot of the email shared online by Azi Paybarah, a former Washington Post reporter now with Straight Arrow News. “I dedicated my life to keeping our families safe-working in the shadows, hunting down terrorists, and standing on the frontlines of our national security.” He then added, in a section of the email highlighted in bold type: “I saw the dead body of Osama bin Laden with my own eyes, knowing that together, we had delivered justice for America.” Rogers, however, was not in Abbottabad, Pakistan on 1 May 2011, when bin Laden was shot and killed, nor was he in the White House Situation Room, where then president Barack Obama, and senior administration officials including Joe Biden and Hillary Clinton followed the raid in real time. Instead, as Rogers told reporters the next day, and recounts in a campaign video, he was at home in Washington DC, where, as the chair of the House intelligence committee at the time, he was informed about the raid in a phone call from Obama’s CIA director, Leon Panetta. While the Rogers campaign did not respond to requests to explain what the former congressman meant by his claim, Paybarah, who first reported the fundraising email sent by Rogers on Sunday, suggested that Rogers must have been referring to the fact that he was one of a select few US officials to have seen a photograph of Bin Laden’s dead body. Days after the raid, Rogers said that the photograph he’d seen made it clear that Bin Laden was dead but supported Obama’s decision to not make the graphic images of the raid public. “The risks of release outweigh the benefits,” Rogers said in a statement at the time. “Conspiracy theorists around the world will just claim the photos are doctored anyway, and there is a real risk that releasing the photos will only serve to inflame public opinion in the Middle East.” The week after the raid, Rogers explained that he had first been informed that the CIA suspected Bin Laden might have been hiding in Pakistan by Panetta four months earlier, when he became chair of the House intelligence committee in January 2011. “At that time”, Rogers recalled at a Council on Foreign Relations event, “it was, a 40 to 50% shot that that was who it was.” As the intelligence got more solid, Rogers said, the CIA director “was very good about keeping us in the loop”. To support the mission, Rogers said, the congressional committee “had to move some money”. In the years since, though, Rogers has frequently referred to his role as a congressman who helped provide funds for US intelligence agencies in vague terms that seemed to exaggerate his role. In the trailer for a CNN series he hosted in 2017, for instance, Rogers introduced himself this way: “My name is Mike Rogers. I oversaw all 16 of our nation’s intelligence agencies”. While an on-screen graphic flashed up that identified him as a “former chair of the House intelligence committee”, a casual viewer might well have assumed tha
